title: How to Repair Your Credit Score in 90 Days: A Practical Action Plan

scenes.text: A ninety-day credit reset starts with one uncomfortable truth: nobody can honestly promise how many points your score will gain, or when. But you can use those ninety days to correct mistakes, prevent new damage, and reduce balances that may be holding your score down.
scenes.subject: credit consultation

scenes.text: Picture doing this at your kitchen table, not paying a stranger for a secret shortcut. The strongest starting tools are already available. Build your plan around three jobs: check your reports, protect your payments, and lower your reported balances. Everything else comes after that.
scenes.subject: kitchen budgeting

scenes.text: During your first week, request your credit reports through AnnualCreditReport.com, the federally authorized website. Free weekly online reports are available from all three bureaus. Those bureaus are Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Review each report separately, because an account or mistake might appear on only one of them.
scenes.subject: laptop credit reports

scenes.text: Your credit report is the underlying record; your credit score is a calculation using that information. Checking your own credit does not hurt it. Write down a starting score, its date, and its scoring model if available. Different models can produce different numbers from your credit information.

visual.headline: YOUR CREDIT REPORT IS THE UNDERLYING RECORD;

scenes.subject: consumer credit check

scenes.text: For meaningful comparisons, follow the same score source over time. A score in one app may differ from the version a lender uses. Next, inspect identifying information, account ownership, balances, limits, and payment history. Highlight anything unfamiliar, inaccurate, or listed more than once without an explanation. Do not automatically dispute every negative item. Accurate negative information generally cannot be removed simply because it makes borrowing harder or feels unfair.

visual.headline: FOR MEANINGFUL COMPARISONS, FOLLOW THE SAME SCORE

scenes.subject: credit score app

scenes.text: Most negative information can remain for seven years, and some bankruptcies for ten. Your ninety-day goal is progress, not erasing an accurate history. If you find a genuine error, gather proof before submitting a dispute. Useful evidence might include payment confirmations, account statements, or identity documents.

visual.headline: MOST NEGATIVE INFORMATION CAN REMAIN FOR SEVEN

scenes.subject: financial records

scenes.text: Dispute the specific error with each bureau reporting it, and contact the company supplying that information. Clearly explain what should change and why. Keep copies and submission dates. Credit bureaus generally investigate disputes within thirty days, though certain circumstances can extend that period to forty-five days.
scenes.subject: dispute letter

scenes.text: Put follow-up dates on your calendar immediately. Review the investigation result and the updated report, rather than assuming a submitted dispute means a correction. An account you never opened deserves special attention. Use IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan, and consider freezing your credit at all three bureaus.

visual.headline: PUT FOLLOW-UP DATES ON YOUR CALENDAR IMMEDIATELY

scenes.subject: followup calendar

scenes.text: A credit freeze is free and helps restrict new-account access to your credit file. It does not erase existing debt or raise your score. Now prevent fresh damage. Make a complete list of account due dates, minimum payments, and any amounts already overdue before deciding on extra payments. Your first payment priority is protecting accounts from becoming newly late. Improving an old problem while creating a new delinquency can undermine your progress.
scenes.subject: credit freeze application

scenes.text: A payment is generally reported as late once it reaches thirty days past due. Fees or other consequences can happen before that point. If an account is approaching that threshold, contact the issuer promptly. Ask what payment is required to keep it from becoming further delinquent.

visual.headline: A PAYMENT IS GENERALLY REPORTED AS LATE

scenes.subject: overdue statement

scenes.text: Set automatic minimum payments when your checking balance can reliably cover them. Add reminders, because an empty account can turn automation into another problem. Use two layers of protection: automatic minimums and a reminder to review each bill. Automation handles timing; your review catches mistakes and spending.
scenes.subject: autopay setup

scenes.text: If minimum payments are unaffordable, ask about hardship options before missing another payment. Confirm fees, account restrictions, and credit reporting before accepting a plan. For complicated debt, a reputable nonprofit credit counselor can review your budget. Nonprofit status alone is not enough; check services, costs, and reputation.

visual.headline: IF MINIMUM PAYMENTS ARE UNAFFORDABLE, ASK ABOUT

scenes.subject: hardship assistance

scenes.text: Next comes credit card utilization: how much of your available revolving credit you are using. High reported balances can weigh on many scoring models. For example, a nine-hundred-dollar reported balance on a card with a three-thousand-dollar limit equals thirty percent utilization. That is arithmetic, not a target. Thirty percent is not a magic safe line. Lower reported utilization generally helps, and scoring can consider both individual cards and your overall balances.
scenes.subject: cardholder budgeting

scenes.text: Do not drain your emergency cushion just to chase a number. A lower balance is useful; needing to borrow immediately for groceries defeats the purpose. After covering every minimum, consider directing extra money toward a nearly maxed-out card. For interest savings, the highest-rate balance is often the better priority.

visual.headline: DO NOT DRAIN YOUR EMERGENCY CUSHION JUST

scenes.subject: grocery shopper

scenes.text: Your payment due date and statement closing date do different jobs. The due date protects payment timing; the closing date often affects reported balances. Many issuers report around the statement closing date, but schedules vary. Ask your issuer when it usually sends balance information to the bureaus.
scenes.subject: statement date review

scenes.text: Paying before that reporting point may produce a lower reported balance. It does not replace making the required payment by your actual due date. You do not need to carry interest-bearing debt to build credit. Paying your statement balance in full can support healthy credit without unnecessary interest.
scenes.subject: early card payment

scenes.text: By the end of your first month, aim for a repeatable system: disputes documented, due dates protected, and a realistic plan for reducing balances. During the second month, verify that payments posted and balances updated. Reporting takes time, so a payment today may not change tomorrow's displayed score.

visual.headline: BY THE END OF YOUR FIRST MONTH,

scenes.subject: monthly budget review

scenes.text: Keep spending below what you can repay. Removing a saved card from shopping apps can create a useful pause before another impulse purchase. Review subscriptions and recurring charges for expenses you no longer use. Redirect actual savings toward debt instead of assuming your budget will somehow stretch. Be cautious about closing an older card solely because its balance is paid off. Losing that available limit can increase your overall utilization.
scenes.subject: online shopper

scenes.text: That does not mean keeping an expensive or tempting card forever. Weigh annual fees, overspending risk, and possible no-fee product changes with your issuer. A higher credit limit can lower utilization if spending stays unchanged. Before requesting one, ask whether the issuer will make a hard credit inquiry.

visual.headline: THAT DOES NOT MEAN KEEPING AN EXPENSIVE

scenes.subject: card fee review

scenes.text: Avoid opening several accounts to chase quick improvements. Applications can add hard inquiries, and new accounts can reduce the average age of your accounts. If you have little or no usable credit, a secured card may help establish history. Look for affordable fees and reporting to all three bureaus.
scenes.subject: credit application

scenes.text: The security deposit is not your monthly payment. Charge only what you can afford, and pay on time under the card's normal billing rules. Becoming an authorized user may help if that account is reported and managed well. High balances or missed payments can also make it unhelpful.
scenes.subject: secured cardholder

scenes.text: Never assume another person's account is a guaranteed shortcut. Confirm reporting and expectations first, and avoid paying strangers for access to their credit history. Collections require a separate decision process. Verify the debt, the amount, and who owns it before sharing payment information or agreeing to a settlement. A collector's validation notice explains important dispute rights and deadlines. Read it promptly, and keep communications organized rather than relying on a phone conversation.

visual.headline: NEVER ASSUME ANOTHER PERSON'S ACCOUNT IS A

scenes.subject: authorized user agreement

scenes.text: With older debt, check your state's rules before acknowledging it or making a payment. In some states, certain actions can restart the lawsuit deadline. That lawsuit deadline is different from the credit reporting time limit. Get qualified legal guidance when the debt's age or legal status is unclear.

visual.headline: WITH OLDER DEBT, CHECK YOUR STATE'S RULES

scenes.subject: legal aid consultation

scenes.text: Paying a collection does not automatically delete it. Scoring treatment varies by model and debt type, so do not count on a specific increase. Before settling, get the agreement in writing, including how the remaining balance will be handled. Afterward, retain proof and check that reporting is accurate.

visual.headline: PAYING A COLLECTION DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY DELETE

scenes.subject: collection payment review

scenes.text: Do not ignore a court summons while working on your score. Legal deadlines need immediate attention, even when a debt does not appear on reports. Now watch for credit repair traps. A company promising a guaranteed score jump or removal of accurate information is selling certainty it cannot deliver.

visual.headline: DO NOT IGNORE A COURT SUMMONS WHILE

scenes.subject: court summons

scenes.text: You can dispute credit report errors yourself for free. Be especially wary of upfront payment demands, false identity schemes, or instructions to invent disputes. During your third month, review the same score source and pull fresh reports. Look for corrected information, lower balances, and uninterrupted on-time payments. If an error remains, read the investigation explanation carefully. Additional evidence may support another dispute; an unresolved problem may justify a consumer complaint.

visual.headline: YOU CAN DISPUTE CREDIT REPORT ERRORS YOURSELF

scenes.subject: scam message

scenes.text: You can submit eligible credit reporting complaints through the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Keep the issue specific and include the records supporting your concern. At day ninety, measure actions as well as points: fewer overdue accounts, smaller revolving balances, corrected errors, and a payment routine you can sustain.

visual.headline: YOU CAN SUBMIT ELIGIBLE CREDIT REPORTING COMPLAINTS

scenes.subject: consumer complaint submission

scenes.text: If high utilization was your main problem, lower reported balances may help relatively quickly. Serious delinquencies usually require more time and consistent positive history. A small score change does not mean the work failed. Scoring models weigh your entire file, and different starting situations produce very different results.

visual.headline: IF HIGH UTILIZATION WAS YOUR MAIN PROBLEM,

scenes.subject: debt payoff tracker

scenes.text: If a major loan application is approaching, avoid last-minute credit experiments. Ask the lender which actions could affect qualification before opening or closing accounts. Remember that approval involves more than a credit score. Income, existing debts, loan requirements, and other underwriting factors can influence the final lending decision.

visual.headline: IF A MAJOR LOAN APPLICATION IS APPROACHING,

scenes.subject: loan officer

scenes.text: Keep the system running after ninety days. Review statements, protect due dates, and use credit only at a level your real budget supports. The practical win is not a secret trick. It is a cleaner record, less avoidable interest, and fewer financial surprises waiting in your mailbox. Which is your biggest obstacle right now: high balances, missed payments, or a report error? Tell us in the comments, and like the video.
scenes.subject: household planning
